**The Weight of a Name**

The first time I heard my name spoken aloud, it was in a voice I didn’t recognize. My mother’s lips moved, but the sound that came out was foreign—soft, hesitant, like she was testing it on for size. I was three years old, sitting on the edge of the bathtub, my toes curling against the cold porcelain. She had just written it in looping script on a piece of paper, tracing the letters with her finger. *"This is you,"* she said, as if naming me was a kind of magic, a way to claim me before the world could forget.

I didn’t know then that names are more than sounds. They are the first stories we are given, the ones we carry like secret passwords. My name—*Elara*—means "radiant" in Greek, though I never asked my mother why she chose it. Maybe it was the way the sun looked through the trees in the summer, or the way her own name, *Lena*, had always felt too quiet for the sky. Or maybe it was just a whim, the kind of thing people do when they are young and believe words can shape the world.

Years later, I would learn that names can also be weapons. In the schoolyard, a boy with a mouth like a rusted hinge called me *"Elara the Alien"* because I wore glasses and had a habit of talking to myself. In college, a professor dismissed my ideas mid-sentence, his pen scratching against the paper like a rat in a cage. *"You don’t sound like someone who would understand this,"* he said. I didn’t argue. I just nodded and sat back, my fingers tightening around my pen until the ink bled through.

I thought about my mother’s voice, the way it had once been warm and sure. Now, it was a ghost in the static.

---

The first time I left the country, I didn’t tell anyone my name. I used an alias, a borrowed identity that let me slip through borders like a shadow. It was easier that way. People didn’t ask questions when you weren’t *Elara*. They didn’t expect you to know things. They didn’t look at you like you were a puzzle they couldn’t solve.

But names are sticky things. They cling to you like sweat on a summer night. When I finally returned, my passport had my real name stamped across the cover, and the world didn’t forget. It just remembered differently.

My mother, when she saw me again, didn’t ask why I’d been gone. She just held my face in her hands and said, *"You’re still here."* It was the first time I realized how much she had been waiting.

---

I write now because names are not just sounds. They are the way we are seen—or unseen. The way we are loved—or left behind. My name is Elara, but it could have been anything. It could have been *Ashley* or *Jamal* or *Mira*. It could have been *Nobody*.

But it isn’t.

And so I keep writing, because words are the only things that stay with us when the rest of the world moves on.

---

**The Weight of a Name (Part II: The Other Side)**

There are names that are given, and names that are taken.

I took mine.

It wasn’t the first time I’d done it. Names are easy to steal when you’re young and hungry for something that feels like yours. I was twelve when I started calling myself *Lark*. It was a bird, I told myself. Light. Free. The kind of thing that could fly away if it wanted to.

My mother didn’t notice at first. She was too busy noticing the other things—how I stopped eating, how I started locking my door, how I carried a knife in my backpack like it was a promise.

*"You’re not a bird,"* she said one night, her voice rough as gravel. *"You’re my daughter."*

I didn’t answer. I just watched the way the light hit the blade of the knife, the way it caught the gold in the handle like a stolen thing.

Names are like that. They can be stolen, too.

---

The first time I heard *Lark* spoken by someone else, it wasn’t in a mirror. It was in a voice I didn’t recognize—deep, rough, the kind of voice that belonged to a man who had seen too much.

*"You’re late,"* he said, and I knew he wasn’t talking about time.

I was nineteen. I had been running for years. Running from the name that had been given me, running from the one I had taken, running from the way my mother’s eyes followed me like a ghost.

He didn’t ask why I was there. He just handed me a cigarette and a key, and said, *"You’re Lark now. That’s all you need to know."*

I took the cigarette. I took the key. I took the name.

And for the first time in years, I didn’t feel like I was running.

---

Names are not just words. They are the way we are seen—or unseen. The way we are loved—or left behind.

I am Elara. I am Lark. I am the girl who stole her own name and the woman who finally learned to keep it.

And sometimes, when the world is too loud, I wonder what my mother would say if she knew.

But she doesn’t.

And that’s okay.

---
